HEADLINE: France dodges rerun of looting and riots after security boost
STANDFIRST: "French government deployed some 70,000 security officials, including elite anti-terror forces"

WHY THIS FILE EXISTS: it is the SECOND APPROVED SOURCE for the France protest story and it RESOLVES the BBC's crowd figures by breaking them down. It does NOT carry the 1,300-plus arrest figure.

CROWD FIGURES — THE BBC'S 410,000 IS NOW EXPLAINED, NOT CONTRADICTED
- Interior ministry, via Irish Times: ABOUT 110,000 in the mostly peaceful Paris demonstration, which was confined to the edge of Paris, plus ANOTHER 300,000 across the rest of the country. 110,000 + 300,000 = 410,000, which is exactly the BBC's national ministry figure. The two outlets agree.
- Union figure: the CGT put it at 800,000. The BBC said "the unions" put it at about 800,000. Agreement again, and the Irish Times names the union.
- SO THERE IS NO CONFLICT ON CROWD SIZE between BBC and Irish Times — only the usual ministry-versus-union gap of 410,000 against 800,000. Print both, attributed, never averaged.
- Last week's comparison: the Irish Times says the 17 October demonstrations "drew more than half a million people".

A REAL CONFLICT — BARCELONA ARRESTS
- BBC: "more than 120 people were arrested" in Barcelona after a student protest.
- Irish Times: "about 100 people were arrested" in Barcelona.
TWO SOURCES, TWO NUMBERS: BBC more than 120, Irish Times about 100. Do not average. If you need one, say "about 100 to 120, depending on the source", or just use one with attribution.

POLICING — AGREES WITH THE BBC ON 70,000
- Some 70,000 security officials deployed, including elite anti-terror forces.
- Soldiers brought in to guard sensitive buildings; helicopters and armoured vehicles known as "centaurs" made available Saturday. Some cities banned protests and extended curfews.
- Museums including the Louvre were closed; many shops were boarded up.
- "While the level of violence toward the police was again high", Nunez said authorities prevented the looting of shops and damage to buildings seen on 17 October.

NAMED QUOTES — ALL NEW, NONE IN THE BBC PIECE
- Laurent Nunez, French Interior Minister, late on Saturday: "All the warning signs were there so that we put in a place a significant presence. We will of course remain fully focused in the days and weeks ahead to face up to this threat, because it is a threat."
- Nunez blamed the clashes on the ULTRA-LEFT, which he said was seeking to "start and finish the uprising". NOTE: in the BBC piece Nunez blames "several thousand radical activists ... including around 500 individuals identified as rioters". The Irish Times gives the political labelling, the BBC gives the arithmetic. Both are his words via different wires.
- Emmanuel Macron, President of France, on Thursday, acknowledged "planning failings and elements of surprise".
- Nathanael Combary, of the Renouveau Lyceen high school union, which is due to meet Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on MONDAY, speaking to the Sunday newspaper La Tribune Dimanche: "The period of dialogue has lasted long enough. We now expect action." LA TRIBUNE DIMANCHE IS NOT IN SOURCES.md — cite the Irish Times reporting it.
- The CGT union, in a statement: "The anger is immense, and our determination is even greater. The government and employers must urgently respond to our social demands."

FORWARD DIARY — USEFUL, AND WE DO NOT HAVE IT ELSEWHERE
- The Renouveau Lyceen union meets Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on MONDAY 26 OCTOBER.
- Labour unions are calling for a MAJOR DAY OF STRIKES AND PROTESTS ON 5 NOVEMBER, and the CGT has pledged to expand the movement until its demands are met.
- Saturday's protests were framed as "Acte II" of the movement, which "still has majority support in polls".

ORIGINS OF THE MOVEMENT
- Began last month with high schoolers blockading establishments, calling for more teachers, repairs to buildings and an end to Parcoursup, the computerised college admissions system.

POLITICS AND MARKETS CONTEXT — DO NOT USE AS A MARKETS ITEM, EXCHANGES ARE SHUT
- An Ipsos-BVA-Cesi Ecole d'ingenieurs survey for Le Parisien published Saturday: the far-right candidate (Marine Le Pen) still firmly leads ahead of next April's presidential election, while Jean-Luc Melenchon of France Unbowed has had a boost from the unrest and stands SECOND, ahead of various centrist competitors. Poll of 1,500 adults, online, 21-22 October. IPSOS IS APPROVED; Le Parisien is not — cite the Irish Times.
- "a closely-watched gauge of bond risk" has been pushed "to levels last seen during the euro-area debt crisis". No number given — do not invent a spread.
- France "dodged a downgrade at Moody's Ratings late on Friday, but the company warned that the widespread protests 'could constrain fiscal consolidation efforts'." Moody's is not in SOURCES.md; cite the Irish Times.
- Preliminary Q3 GDP is due FRIDAY; analysts expect expansion of just 0.1 per cent after zero growth in the previous quarter. FORECAST, not data.

ELSEWHERE IN EUROPE
- About 100 arrested in Barcelona amid a heavy police presence, with scattered clashes.
- Tirana, Albania "continued to be rocked by demonstrations against its prime minister."

OMITTED DELIBERATELY: the piece notes a Paris Saint-Germain v Olympique Lyonnais match was postponed. That is sport and our rules bar sports content anywhere on the site. Do not use it, even as colour.
